newsitem.title: UK: Quality and price key to German oil sale - traders.
newsitem.headline: Quality and price key to German oil sale - traders.

text.p: Most of Germany's government-controlled strategic oil reserves due to be sold to help trim the budget deficit will go to the country's own refiners if the price and quality are right, industry sources said on Friday.

EBV, the Hamburg-based agency handling the sale, will begin lifting the crude oil from underground salt caverns on Monday and will be ready to sell the first tranche of about 2.8 million barrels 10 days later.
"There will be a bidding process which will give buyers the chance to sample the oil, which is vital," said a German refinery executive.

"We are interested in the oil but it depends on our supply situation and the quality and we are waiting for the first volume which will give us a good basis for determining that," said the head of crude supply for a German oil company.

Oil traders said they expected the bulk of the crude to go to refineries in Germany or the Antwerp-Rotterdam-Amsterdam (ARA) region via a comprehensive pipeline network, bypassing the need to ship cargoes from the north German port of Wilhelmshaven.

A large proportion of the oil is thought to be high-sulphur or sour crude, including grades from the Middle East like Iranian Heavy and Arab Heavy and Russian Urals, which usually commands lower prices than world benchmark North Sea Brent.

The crude, which has been in storage since the late 1970s when it was stockpiled to protect Europe's most oil import-dependent economy from further price shocks, may also have lost value due to contamination.
"I would expect most of it to go to the German refiners if the price is right but who knows what the mineral content is like. It could be fairly salty," said a trader.
Traders were also concerned about vaporisation, another problem associated with crude oil stored under lower pressure than its original reservoir, and its metals content.
"It's possible that some of the lighter ends (components) of the crude could have formed a gas cap at the top," said a senior trader.
"If you draw down on them you may find the API (gravity) is heavier than first thought," he added.
German government sources said 45 percent of the reserves was heavy crude with an average gravity of 30.5 degrees API.
If the crude has deteriorated substantially, then Bonn will be forced to sell a greater volume to reach the 400 million marks revenue target set for 1997 and the 500 million marks target for 1998.
Substantial discounts to benchmark physical Dated Brent, trading on Friday at about $18.05 a barrel, were already being discussed.
"The discounts will certainly be much bigger than $1," said a trader.
If EBV manages to achieve $17 a barrel, seen as optimistic by many market sources, Germany will have to sell an average of 80,000 bpd for the balance of this year.

Although small in relation to the European market, the displacement of a similar quantity of Russian Urals, particularly if it coincides with a resumption of Iraqi exports, would depress spot sour crudes.
"If Iraq comes back and if this is flowing there will be ample supplies of sour crude around in August," said a trader.
